item.title: The Child’s Bath
item.lesson: Mary Cassatt, a Pennsylvania banker's daughter who moved to Paris over her family's objections, was the only American ever invited to exhibit with the Impressionists — recruited personally by Degas after he saw her Salon work. Barred by propriety from the cafés and backstages where her male colleagues found their subjects, she claimed domestic life as territory for serious art and made it modern. This, her masterpiece, shows a woman washing a child's feet — an everyday intimacy composed with radical means borrowed from the Japanese prints she collected: the viewpoint plunging from above, bold pattern crowding pattern (stripes, florals, carpet), perspective flattened like a woodblock. The mother's hand circles the child's foot with the exact firm tenderness anyone who has bathed a child knows. Sentimental subject, rigorous picture: that combination — feeling held in structural discipline — is Cassatt's signature, and a rebuke to anyone who filed 'mothers and children' under minor art.
item.lookFor: Notice both faces point down at the basin — neither performs for us. We watch attention itself: the picture's subject is not the bath but the absorption of two people in one small task.
